fixes.find: Two years of mining college I sat through for one piece of paper, and in September of '09 they hand it to me.
fixes.replace: I sat through two years of mining college for one piece of paper, and in September of '09 they hand it to me.
fixes.why: Inversion copies Russian word order; the straightforward English sentence keeps the voice without sounding translated.

fixes.find: That's exactly what it says in my employment book now
fixes.replace: That's exactly what it says in my work record book now
fixes.why: "Employment book" is opaque in English; "work record book" is clearer while preserving the Russian realia.

fixes.find: You hand a tin tag through the window and get a cap lamp and a self-rescuer, an iron can on a belt that gives you half an hour of air when there's nothing around you to breathe.
fixes.replace: You hand a tin tag through the window and get a cap lamp and a self-rescuer, a metal canister on your belt that gives you half an hour of air when there's nothing around you to breathe.
fixes.why: "Iron can" sounds literal and clumsy; a self-rescuer is a metal canister.

fixes.find: "Brought it back. Good boy."
fixes.replace: "Brought it back. Good job."
fixes.why: "Good boy" infantilizes adult miners more than Russian "молодец" does.

fixes.find: We've crawled out from under the same roof once already… Not in this life
fixes.replace: We've crawled out from under the same cave-in once already… Not in this life
fixes.why: "Under the same roof" reads as a domestic idiom, not a mine-roof collapse.

fixes.find: I follow Dad around like a tail, and he doesn't chase me off.
fixes.replace: I follow Dad everywhere, and he doesn't chase me off.
fixes.why: "Like a tail" is a Russian idiom carried over too literally.

fixes.find: Underground he talks more than he does at home in a week, and all of it to the point.
fixes.replace: Underground he talks more than he does at home in a week, and every word is about the job.
fixes.why: "All of it to the point" is not idiomatic English for "всё по делу."

fixes.find: he scrubs my back with a washcloth like when I was little, silently and hard.
fixes.replace: he scrubs my back hard with a washcloth, like when I was little, without a word.
fixes.why: "Silently and hard" is an awkward adverb pairing.

fixes.find: The tag is hanging from her hand.
fixes.replace: The tag is in her hand.
fixes.why: A tag held by someone is "in" her hand; "hanging from" misplaces the image.

fixes.find: She doesn't give it back right away, and in the second week she pours me tea from her thermos on top of it, strong and sweet like on a train.
fixes.replace: She doesn't give it back right away, and in the second week she also pours me tea from her thermos, strong and sweet like on a train.
fixes.why: "On top of it" accidentally sounds as if she pours tea onto the tag.

fixes.find: the father's at the face, and the son runs off to his buddy.
fixes.replace: his father is at the face, and he's running off to his buddy.
fixes.why: The article pattern copies Russian proverbial phrasing and sounds unnatural here.

fixes.find: Night shift, the third longwall, past four in the morning.
fixes.replace: Night shift, the third longwall, fourth hour.
fixes.why: "Четвёртый час" here is the fourth hour of the shift, not simply clock time after four.

fixes.find: Coal shoots at the Glubokaya every week
fixes.replace: Coal shoots at Glubokaya every week
fixes.why: After the mine has been introduced, the bare mine name is more natural than "the Glubokaya."

fixes.find: I look at it, and it looks back at me, I think.
fixes.replace: I look at it, and it seems to look back.
fixes.why: The tag-on "I think" weakens the line and creates a clumsy comma-splice feel.

fixes.find: The coal flows down the face like water
fixes.replace: The coal flows along the face like water
fixes.why: The coal moves along the longwall, not vertically "down" the face.

fixes.find: "Forty years I've been listening to her. How did you hear her, Samokhin?"
fixes.replace: "Forty years I've been listening to it. How did you hear it, Samokhin?"
fixes.why: The Russian refers to the seam/stratum; the added feminine personification is not motivated in English.

fixes.find: "Brought it back," she says. "Good boy."
fixes.replace: "Brought it back," she says. "Good job."
fixes.why: As in the earlier refrain, "Good boy" is too infantilizing.

fixes.find: thin, like the puppy he was at the backwater.
fixes.replace: thin, the way he did as a puppy by the backwater.
fixes.why: The original phrasing is syntactically awkward and blurs sound with identity.

fixes.find: The rubber is sour, breathing through it is tight.
fixes.replace: The rubber tastes sour, and each breath comes hard.
fixes.why: "Breathing is tight" is a literal calque; the revised line is physical English.

fixes.find: "What's got into you, Samokhin? She's only shooting."
fixes.replace: "What's got into you, Samokhin? It's only shooting."
fixes.why: Again, "she" adds an English personification not present or needed here.

fixes.find: Dying, it turns out, isn't something I can manage. What I can manage is remembering how I died, and going to work with that.
fixes.replace: Apparently I can't manage dying. I remember how I died, and I carry that with me to work.
fixes.why: This falls into the "not X but Y" pattern and sounds more essayistic than the narrator.

fixes.find: Sometimes at lunch I suddenly feel coal between my teeth and wash it down with stewed-fruit juice for a long time.
fixes.replace: Sometimes at lunch I suddenly feel coal between my teeth and spend a long time washing it down with the sweet stewed-fruit drink.
fixes.why: "Stewed-fruit juice" is not idiomatic; the replacement explains компот without a footnote.

fixes.find: at the Glubokaya it beeps all the time
fixes.replace: at Glubokaya it beeps all the time
fixes.why: The mine name reads more naturally without the article after first mention.

fixes.find: over the sleepers
fixes.replace: over the rail ties
fixes.why: "Sleepers" is British railway vocabulary; the style guide uses American spelling and neutral English.

fixes.find: My body is strong; it has enough for this.
fixes.replace: My body's strong; it can take this.
fixes.why: "It has enough for this" copies Russian "его хватает" too literally.

fixes.find: "You rat, you could've at least called me."
fixes.replace: "You rat, you could've at least yelled for me."
fixes.why: In context he means shouting a warning, not phoning or generally calling.

fixes.find: Cold air pulls through the gap, a real fresh current from the next drift, and I sit by that gap until the rescuers come.
fixes.replace: A cold draft comes through the gap, a real fresh current from the next drift, and I sit there until the rescuers come.
fixes.why: "Air pulls through" is a Russian-style construction; "draft comes through" is natural.

fixes.find: Here, at the Glubokaya, methane collects up top
fixes.replace: Here, at Glubokaya, methane collects up top
fixes.why: Same article issue with the mine name.

fixes.find: On the third try it gives, and cold air pulls through the gap, a real fresh current.
fixes.replace: On the third try it gives, and a cold draft comes through the gap, a real fresh current.
fixes.why: Same unidiomatic "air pulls through" construction.

fixes.find: Up at the roof the gas detector chokes; down at the floor it beeps every other second.
fixes.replace: Up by the roof the gas detector goes frantic; down by the floor it beeps on and off.
fixes.why: "Every other second" invents a precise timing not in "пищит через раз," and "goes frantic" better fits the detector.

fixes.find: The crosscut comes out on a different current, from a different fan.
fixes.replace: The crosscut opens onto a different air current, from a different fan.
fixes.why: "Comes out on a current" is not idiomatic; "opens onto" is clearer.

fixes.find: and in it is an iron door, small, chest-high
fixes.replace: and in it is a steel door, small, chest-high
fixes.why: English would normally call this a steel door; "iron" is a literal rendering of железная.

fixes.find: In front of the door is a rock fall from the roof, knee-deep, and the door is wedged against it.
fixes.replace: In front of the door is knee-deep fallen rock from the roof, and the door is wedged against it.
fixes.why: "A rock fall" is awkward here; the physical obstacle is fallen rock.

fixes.find: The door sits as if it had grown there.
fixes.replace: The door is stuck fast.
fixes.why: The literal image sounds translated; the scene needs the immediate physical fact.

fixes.find: From under it, through the gap at the floor, comes the cold, damp air of the next drift, and I hold my palm under the gap like under a tap.
fixes.replace: Cold, damp air from the next drift comes through the gap under it, down by the floor, and I hold my palm under the gap as if under a faucet.
fixes.why: The inversion and "like under a tap" are stiff; this keeps the action readable.

fixes.find: On the other side there's a draft like from an open window in winter
fixes.replace: On the other side there's a draft as cold as an open window in winter
fixes.why: "Like from" is unidiomatic; the comparison needs to be recast.

fixes.find: he slaps my helmet:
fixes.replace: he slaps me on the helmet:
fixes.why: In English you slap a person on the helmet, not usually the helmet alone in this construction.

fixes.find: and breathe that gap for as long as I can.
fixes.replace: and breathe through that gap for as long as I can.
fixes.why: "Breathe that gap" is a Russian calque; English needs "through."

verdict: В целом партия крепкая: шахтёрская среда читается материально, темп хороший, голос двадцатилетнего в основном выдержан. Чаще всего мешают кальки с русской синтаксики, буквальные горные/бытовые реалии вроде iron can или rock fall, и мелкие английские сочетаемостные сбои. Отдельно стоит выровнять обращения и рефрен Тани: "Good boy" уводит сцену не туда.
